doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: No unions or days off; downtown Local 802
summary: Early New York jobs had no unions or vacations; he marched for them and hung out downtown.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: You had to start work at six at Ryan’s?
You started at six o’clock. How late did you have to play then?
Well during those days, when you say how late did you have to play, there wasn’t any unions, there wasn’t any days off, there wasn’t any vacation. When I first came to New

York there wasn’t any vacations, there wasn’t any unions or anything like that. As a matter of fact, I marched for the day off. I marched for unions, and at that particular time 802 was always — it wasn’t segregated — but it was like uptown, downtown you know. The majority of the black musicians hung out at a place called The Rhythm Club downtown, and the white musicians were on the floor. But for just one reason I hung out downtown, and I would say since I’m interviewing you, I would say that if you look it up, in some of those look up books, and I have the pictures and everything, I was with one of the first integrated bands in the country. The first one was, I think we all — you’ll have to look in your jazz books — the first one was by a fine band leader called Boyd Raeburn. Maybe you’ve heard of him, a saxophone player.
